summary: Examines address-scanning attacks in IPv6. The huge subnet size makes brute-force scanning look impractical, but this document discusses how attackers can still find hosts and what that means for security.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 has far more addresses than IPv4, but many hosts use patterns that reduce the number an attacker must check. RFC 7707 describes these patterns and other ways to discover addresses, along with steps that can make scanning harder.

questions: how do attackers find hosts in ipv6
how to prevent ipv6 address scanning
what are low byte ipv6 addresses
how do address patterns make ipv6 hosts easier to find
subtitle: Why predictable IPv6 addresses and other network information can make reconnaissance possible.

tldr.problem: A /64 IPv6 subnet has a large address space, but common address patterns and other information sources can make hosts easier to find than brute-force scanning suggests.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines address-generation patterns, remote and local scanning, and other ways to learn addresses, then lists mitigations such as unpredictable addresses and filtering.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7707 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 5157. It concludes that scanning is less feasible than in IPv4, but heuristics and other reconnaissance methods can still help find hosts.

today: RFC 7707 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 5157. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: IPv6 Scanning Is Difficult but Possible
sections.content:
A typical IPv6 subnet has a 64-bit interface identifier, so testing every possible address is not feasible. RFC 7707 obsoletes RFC 5157 and explains how address patterns can reduce that search space.

The RFC also describes reconnaissance methods that do not rely on guessing every address. It presents the material for security administrators and for people assessing the security of production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Trying every possible IPv6 address would take too much effort. Predictable address choices and other information sources can narrow the search.

sections.title: Address Patterns Reduce the Search Space
sections.content:
With traditional SLAAC, an interface identifier can be based on a network card's hardware address. This can expose vendor information and reduce the search space; the RFC describes cases where a nominal 64-bit space becomes 2^24 or a multiple of 2^24.

Sequential DHCPv6 assignments and manually chosen addresses can also be predictable. The RFC discusses low-byte, IPv4-based, service-port, and word-based address patterns. RFC 7217's stable, semantically opaque identifiers are presented as a way to remove such patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IPv6 addresses include values that are easy to guess, such as hardware-address patterns or small numbers. Less predictable identifiers make it harder to narrow the search.

sections.title: Remote and Local Address Scanning
sections.content:
Brute-force scanning of an entire /64 is not feasible, so remote scans rely on address patterns and likely subnet assignments. The RFC notes that probing many addresses can also create a large neighbor-cache load on the last-hop router and may cause denial of service.

Local scanning differs because an attacker on the link can send probes to the all-nodes link-local multicast address ff02::1. The RFC also describes probe types that may cause hosts to send ICMPv6 error responses.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote scan must narrow the address range first. On a local network, multicast probes can reach many nodes without guessing each unicast address.

sections.title: Other Sources of Address Information
sections.content:
The RFC lists public sources such as DNS records, zone transfers, common host-name lookups, mailing-list archives, peer-to-peer applications, and traceroute results. Reverse DNS under ip6.arpa can also reveal whether addresses have records below a queried part of the tree.

With local access or system credentials, a person may inspect neighbor caches, routing tables, configuration files, logs, routing protocols, IPFIX data, SNMP, or network traffic. These methods show that address discovery is not limited to scanning a remote subnet.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS, public messages, network devices, and traffic can reveal addresses without testing the full IPv6 range. Some sources require local access or login credentials.

sections.title: Mitigations and Conclusions
sections.content:
The RFC recommends avoiding predictable address assignments, using stable semantically opaque interface identifiers where available, and avoiding sequential DHCPv6 addresses. It also lists perimeter intrusion prevention, IPv6 packet filtering, and keeping the default /64 subnet size.

The document cautions that hiding addresses is only one layer of security. Other local reconnaissance methods may remain available even when address-scanning techniques are reduced.
sections.plainLanguage: Use address assignments that are difficult to guess and apply ordinary network protections. Unpredictable addresses are only one part of a broader security approach.
